statement: A CSV field may be enclosed in double quotes; fields containing line breaks, double quotes or commas should be; a double quote inside a quoted field is written as two double quotes. The enclosing quotes and the doubling are syntax, not field data.
location: Section 2, items 5 to 7 and the ABNF (escaped, TEXTDATA)
inference: The bytes of a value inside a quoted CSV field are contiguous and unchanged; the enclosing quote characters are not part of the value, so a span excludes them.

notes: RFC 4180 is Informational and documents common practice; real CSV producers deviate (unquoted quotes, other delimiters), which is not modeled.
Doubled quotes are only unwrapped by a CSV parser; a text-level span over the raw line is unaffected for values that contain none.

statement: Each CSV record is delimited by a line break written CRLF; the last record may omit it. CR and LF may also appear inside an escaped field.
location: Section 2, items 1, 2 and 6, and the ABNF (CRLF, escaped)
inference: A value at the end of a record is followed by CR, which is not part of the value; a span ends before CR. Whether a reader treats a bare LF the same way is not established by this source.

notes: Only the CRLF form is documented; bare LF files are common and out of this source's scope.

statement: A JSON string is delimited by quotation marks; quotation mark, reverse solidus and control characters U+0000 to U+001F must be escaped; any character may be escaped, including as a six-character \uXXXX sequence.
inference: A value inside a JSON string keeps its bytes when it contains no escaped character; the adjacent backslash-quote pairs are syntax. A value written with \uXXXX escapes decodes to the same characters but its text bytes differ, so a text-level span over the encoded bytes is a representation question, not settled by the RFC.

notes: Nested JSON (a JSON document inside a string) adds one escape level per nesting; only one level is exercised.

statement: A percent-encoded octet is written as percent followed by two hexadecimal digits; the at sign is a reserved general delimiter, so it may appear percent-encoded as %40 in a component where it is not meant as the delimiter.
location: Section 2.1 Percent-Encoding and Section 2.2 Reserved Characters (gen-delims)
inference: A mailbox in a URI component can be carried with its at sign encoded; decoding yields the original octets. Whether the encoded form is in scope for an expectation on the raw text is a project decision this source does not make.

notes: Which components a producer encodes, and whether it also double-encodes, is not covered.

statement: When parsing application/x-www-form-urlencoded bytes, each plus sign in a name or value is replaced with a space before percent-decoding.
inference: An unescaped plus sign in a form value is read as a space, so a plus-prefixed international phone number in a query string loses its plus sign unless written as %2B.

notes: Living standard read without recording a commit; wording was matched by search, not by reading the whole section.
Whether a particular producer encoded the plus is unknowable from the text alone.

statement: SMTP internationalization extends atext with UTF8-non-ascii and the sub-domain with U-label, so non-ASCII characters can appear in the local part of an internationalized mailbox.
inference: A non-ASCII character directly after a mailbox is not excluded from the mailbox by the grammar alone; separating sentence punctuation from the address needs context. Treating a trailing ideographic full stop as punctuation or as part of the domain is not decided by this source.

notes: Domain-side handling of non-ASCII dots (IDNA mapping) was not read.
